passage: On Monday, Kunal opened the stock sheet he had sent to Kalyani, a client who ran a small furniture shop, and saw that two columns had swapped, so the prices on it were wrong. His first thought was to fix it quietly and hope she had not used it. On Tuesday he rang her instead. "The sheet I sent has an error. Please do not use it for orders. I can send a corrected one by Thursday noon, and I will add a checking step before every future file." There was a pause. "Thank you for telling me now," Kalyani said. On Friday the corrected sheet had gone out, and Kalyani had placed her orders using it. She asked Kunal to take on the next project.

qa.q: What was wrong with the stock sheet?
qa.a: Two columns had swapped, so the prices on it were wrong.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling on Monday when he first saw the swapped columns?
qa.a: Worried and tempted to hide it, since his first thought was to fix it quietly and hope she had not used it.

qa.q: Why was it better to phone Kalyani on Tuesday?
qa.a: Because Kalyani could avoid orders at the wrong prices, and the corrected sheet and the checking step gave her a real alternative.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel after that call?
qa.a: Grateful and reassured that Kunal told her early, which is why she gave him the next project.

grounding: Illustrates a person who tells a client plainly what went wrong and offers a real fix, so the short-term discomfort stays small.

passage: Chinmay uncle here, so listen. When I was twenty-five and painting signboards, Rafiq, who ran the sweet shop by the bus stand, ordered a big board for his shop's opening on Sunday. By Thursday the paint was still wet and two letters were crooked. I could have hurried and delivered a smudged board. Instead I walked to his shop and said, "It will not be right by Sunday. I can give you a plain banner for the opening, and the proper board on Wednesday, at no extra charge." Rafiq's face fell. He shouted a little. Then he took the banner. On Wednesday he stood back from the new board, and that month he sent three neighbours to me. That Sunday was uncomfortable, but a smudged board would have been worse.

qa.q: What did Chinmay offer Rafiq for the opening on Sunday?
qa.a: Chinmay offered a plain banner for the opening and the proper board on Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Rafiq feel when told the board would not be ready?
qa.a: Disappointed and angry, since his face fell and he shouted a little.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make on Thursday that mattered?
qa.a: Chinmay walked to the shop and told Rafiq honestly, with a real alternative, instead of delivering a smudged board.

qa.q: How might the young Chinmay have seen that uncomfortable Sunday afterwards?
qa.a: Chinmay saw it as a price worth paying, since a smudged board would have been worse and the honest word led Rafiq to send three neighbours.

grounding: Illustrates a person under pressure who says plainly what cannot be done and offers a real alternative, which builds trust.

passage:
At 10:15 on the wedding day, the catering van broke down on the highway outside Lonavala. Dilnaz stood by the roadside in the heat, phone to her ear, as the mechanic shook his head. Lunch was at one. The paneer and the dal were in the van. The rice and desserts had gone ahead in the second vehicle.
She could have told the client, Aparna, "Slight delay, all good," and hoped. Instead she called her straight away.
"Aparna, I have bad news. Our van has broken down. The paneer and dal won't reach by one. The rice, raita and desserts will. I can have a local kitchen near the venue make fresh dal by 12:30, and I'll replace the paneer with a vegetable dish I can cook there. I'll take the extra cost. I'm very sorry."
Silence. Then Aparna said, "Thank you for telling me now. Do it."
The guests ate at 1:15. Nobody asked about the paneer. Aparna tipped the staff.

qa.q: At what time did the catering van break down?
qa.a: At 10:15 on the wedding day.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt making that call?
qa.a: Dilnaz was probably anxious and embarrassed, but determined to be honest before the problem grew.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that turned bad news into trust?
qa.a: Dilnaz called straight away, said exactly what would and wouldn't arrive, offered a real alternative and took the extra cost.

qa.q: How did Aparna react to the news?
qa.a: Aparna was quiet at first, then grateful to be told early, and later tipped the staff.

grounding: Illustrates a caterer under pressure who tells the client plainly what went wrong and offers a real alternative, earning trust.

passage:
In the architecture office in Chennai, Seema, a junior architect, was checking her drawings for a school building when her stomach dropped. The staircase width in her plan was fifteen centimetres short of the code. The drawings had gone to the contractor on Friday.
She could fix the drawing quietly and send a "revised version" without saying why. She thought about it for a full minute.
Then she walked to her manager Santosh's desk. "Santosh, I made an error in the staircase drawings for the school. The width is fifteen centimetres short of the code. I've already redrawn it. The contractor hasn't started the stairs yet; I checked. Can I call them now, with you on the line?"
Santosh looked at the drawing for a long moment. "Good catch. Yes, call them."
The contractor thanked them. Santosh said nothing more about it, but the next month he gave Seema the review of all the junior drawings.

qa.q: How short of the code was the staircase width?
qa.a: Fifteen centimetres short of the code.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she found the error?
qa.a: Seema felt a sick drop of fear, and for a full minute was tempted to fix it quietly.

qa.q: What made Seema's way of reporting the error effective?
qa.a: She stated the mistake plainly, had already redrawn it, had checked the contractor hadn't started and offered to call them at once.

qa.q: How does Santosh see Seema after this?
qa.a: Santosh trusts her more, calling it a good catch and later giving her the review of all the junior drawings.

grounding: Shows a junior architect who tells her manager plainly about a mistake with a ready fix, rather than concealing it.

passage:
"Arohi, got a minute? It's about the manual."
"Salma! Yes, go ahead. All forty pages on track for Friday?"
"That's why I'm calling. No. I'm sorry. My mother was in hospital last week, and I lost four days. I can deliver twenty-five pages, fully checked, by Friday. The last fifteen by Tuesday."
"Tuesday? We present to the client Monday."
"Then there's another option. My colleague Farah translates the same language pair. She could do the last fifteen by Friday, and I'd review them on Saturday for consistency."
"Hmm. Would you trust her work?"
"I've worked with her for three years. Yes."
"Why didn't you just send something rushed?"
"Because you'd find the mistakes on Monday, in front of your client."
A pause. "Okay. Use Farah. And Salma, thank you for not pretending."
"Thank you for hearing it."

qa.q: How many pages can Salma deliver by Friday?
qa.a: Twenty-five pages, fully checked, by Friday.

qa.q: Why did Salma choose not to send something rushed?
qa.a: Salma was worried Arohi would find mistakes on Monday in front of the client, which would hurt more than honesty now.

qa.q: What makes Salma's message a good example of honesty about limits?
qa.a: Salma says plainly what cannot be done, explains why, and offers real alternatives, a later date or a trusted colleague with a review.

qa.q: How does Arohi respond to Salma's honesty?
qa.a: Arohi is briefly worried about the Monday meeting but ends grateful, thanking Salma for not pretending.

grounding: Illustrates a freelancer who tells a client plainly what cannot be done by the deadline and offers a real alternative.

passage:
Last spring I was translating event posters from English into Kannada for Shreya, who ran a small reading charity in Mysuru. Two days before the book fair, I noticed I'd written the venue as the Old Town Hall instead of the Town Hall, two kilometres apart, and five hundred posters were already up.
My first thought was that nobody would notice. My second was a picture of families with small children waiting outside the wrong building.
So I, Chandrika, called Shreya that evening before I lost my nerve. "I made a mistake on the Kannada posters. The venue is wrong. I'm really sorry. I've corrected the file, and I can print a sticker strip tonight and help paste it over the old line tomorrow morning."
There was a long silence. Then she said, "Thank you for telling me now, not after Saturday." We spent Thursday morning on a scooter with a roll of stickers.
My face burned during that call. But I still translate for her, three years later.

qa.q: Which venue did Chandrika wrongly write on the posters?
qa.a: The Old Town Hall instead of the Town Hall.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling during the call to Shreya?
qa.a: Chandrika felt ashamed and nervous, face burning, but made the call before losing nerve.

qa.q: What made Chandrika's call a good way to own the error?
qa.a: Chandrika said plainly what went wrong, apologised, and offered a real fix: a corrected file, stickers printed that night and help pasting them.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika had hoped nobody would notice?
qa.a: Families with small children could have waited outside the wrong building on Saturday, and Shreya might have stopped trusting Chandrika.

grounding: Shows a person telling a client plainly what went wrong under deadline pressure and offering a real fix.
